newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Sugar listing seen boosting tiny Malawi bourse.
newsitem.headline: Sugar listing seen boosting tiny Malawi bourse.

text.p: The expected merger and listing of two Malawi sugar companies later this year is set to boost the southern African country's fledgling stock market, industry sources and analysts said on Friday.
The Malawi government intends to reduce further its shareholding in Dwangwa Sugar Corp and Sugar Corporation Malawi (Sucoma) and plans are afoot to merge the two firms.
Illovo Sugar Ltd owns 49 percent of Dwangwa and 60 percent of Sucoma, after buying the sugar interests of Lonrho Plc in May.
Lonrho Sugar upped its stakes in the companies in February this year, prior to the sale to Illovo. Previously it held 27 percent in Dwangwa and 51 percent of Sucoma.
Industry sources said plans were far advanced for the listing of a merged company on the Malawi stock exchange before the end of the year.
"The Malawi government wants to continue the process of further disposing of some of their shares in the two sugar companies," one industry source said.
The source said Illovo -- as controlling shareholder of Sucoma and a substantial shareholder in Dwangwa -- would support a listing of the Malawi industry on the Malawi exchange.
"In terms of the listing, the fundamentals are all very good. Having a large dominant focused shareholder like Illovo standing behind the thing, will go a long way towards ensuring its success.
"(They) feel it would give a good boost to the stock exchange in that those two sugar businesses are world class.
"A merger between the two companies has certainly been discussed but has not been approved yet by the companies and the shareholders in general meetings," the source added.

A merger between Dwangwa and Sucoma would leave Illovo -- now consolidating its position as an African producer after the Lonrho purchase -- as majority equity holder and in control of the Malawi industry, analysts said.

Industry officials have put the value of the two sugar companies at around two billion Malawi kwacha ($193 million) but analysts have said the value could be as high as $250 million -- making a merged company one of the largest in the region.

Stockbrokers Investec Securities said in a report this week that the listing of the sugar company later in the year could start a process which could lead to more investment and more listings on the bourse.
Investec said the performance of shares of other listed sugar companies in Zambia and Zimbabwe showed "that investors have an appetite for African sugar companies".
With its low cost base and excellent levels of production, a listed Malawi sugar company would be a good investment, Investec said.
"Malawi Sugar could therefore be one of the larger listed companies in the region -- well worth consideration by any African fund manager."
